body:
What is an atom?

All matter is made of atoms. An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains the chemical identity of that element. Atoms are extremely small, but they have an internal structure. The three main subatomic particles are protons, neutrons and electrons.

At the centre of an atom is a tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy the region surrounding the nucleus. Nearly all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus because protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons.

ParticleElectric chargeLocationRelative mass
Proton+1NucleusApproximately 1
Neutron0NucleusApproximately 1
Electron-1Outside the nucleusApproximately 1/1836 of a proton

Protons and electrons have charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign. A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons. Neutrons have no electric charge.

How atomic structure became understood

The discovery of the electron by J. J. Thomson showed that atoms contain smaller particles. Ernest Rutherford established the nuclear model of the atom through alpha-particle scattering: most particles passed through thin gold foil, while a small fraction underwent large deflections. This showed that an atom is mostly empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a very small nucleus.

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons occupy permitted energy levels or shells. At school level, these shells provide a useful way to understand electron arrangement. Actual electron behaviour is more complex than the picture of tiny planets moving around the nucleus.

James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. The common hydrogen-1 atom is an important exception to the general presence of neutrons in nuclei: its nucleus has 1 proton and no neutron.

Atomic number identifies the element

The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus. All atoms of a particular element have the same atomic number.

Hydrogen has 1 proton, so its atomic number is 1. Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6. Oxygen has 8 protons, so its atomic number is 8. Changing the number of protons changes the element itself.

The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. Therefore, A = Z + N, where N is the number of neutrons. Equivalently, N = A - Z.

Carbon-14

Carbon-14 has atomic number 6 and mass number 14. Its nucleus therefore contains 6 protons and 8 neutrons. A neutral carbon-14 atom also has 6 electrons. The number 14 represents its mass number, not its number of neutrons.

Atoms and ions are different

An ion forms when an atom or group of atoms gains or loses electrons. Losing electrons produces a positively charged ion, called a cation. Gaining electrons produces a negatively charged ion, called an anion.

For example, a neutral sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. A sodium ion, Na+, has 11 protons but only 10 electrons. Sodium remains sodium because its proton number is unchanged.

Proton number determines the element; electron number determines whether an atom is electrically neutral or charged. Neutron number distinguishes isotopes of the same element.

Prelims focus

  • Atomic number = number of protons.
  • Mass number = protons + neutrons.
  • A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
  • Rutherford established the nuclear model; Bohr proposed permitted electron energy levels.
  • Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
  • Trap: Losing an electron changes an atom into an ion, not into another element.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, printed pp. 46-54.]

title: The Atom: Subatomic Particles, Atomic Number and Mass Number

body:
Why atoms of the same element can have different masses

The atomic number of an element is fixed because every atom of that element has the same number of protons. However, atoms of the same element can contain different numbers of neutrons. Such atoms are called isotopes.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers. They have equal numbers of protons and different numbers of neutrons.

For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 both contain 6 protons. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 8 neutrons. Both are carbon atoms because their atomic number is 6.

The 3 isotopes of hydrogen

Hydrogen provides a particularly clear example because its common isotopes differ only in the number of neutrons.

IsotopeProtonsNeutronsMass number
Protium (hydrogen-1)101
Deuterium (hydrogen-2)112
Tritium (hydrogen-3)123

All 3 isotopes have atomic number 1. In a neutral state, each also has 1 electron. Protium and deuterium are stable, whereas tritium is radioactive. Deuterium is often called heavy hydrogen. Water containing deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen is known as heavy water when its hydrogen atoms are deuterium.

Similar chemical properties, different nuclear properties

Since isotopes of an element have the same proton number, their neutral atoms also have the same number of electrons. Consequently, they generally show very similar chemical behaviour. Their masses are different, so some physical properties and reaction rates may differ.

Nuclear stability may also differ. Carbon-12 is stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive. Therefore, being an isotope does not automatically mean being radioactive. Every element can have isotopes, and the stability of individual isotopes must be considered separately.

Why the atomic mass in the periodic table may be a decimal

An individual atom has a definite number of protons and neutrons, so its mass number is a whole number. The relative atomic mass shown for an element commonly represents a weighted average of the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes.

For a simplified illustration, chlorine occurs mainly as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. If their relative abundances are approximately 75% and 25%, the weighted average is about 35.5. This does not mean that a chlorine atom contains a fraction of a neutron. It means that a natural sample contains atoms of different isotopes.

Mass number and relative atomic mass are not the same. Mass number counts the protons and neutrons in one nucleus. Relative atomic mass is a mass comparison that can reflect the isotope mixture of an element.

Isobars belong to different elements

Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers. For example, argon-40 has 18 protons and 22 neutrons, whereas calcium-40 has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Both have mass number 40, but they are different elements.

RelationshipWhat is the same?What is different?
IsotopesAtomic numberMass number and neutron number
IsobarsMass numberAtomic number
Neutral atom and its ionProton number and nucleusElectron number and electric charge

Why particular isotopes are useful

Different nuclear properties allow selected isotopes to serve different purposes. Uranium-235 is a nuclear fuel because its nucleus can undergo neutron-induced fission. Cobalt-60 is a radioactive source used in some cancer radiotherapy systems. Iodine-131 is used in particular treatments of thyroid disorders. Carbon-14 is useful for dating some materials of biological origin because it undergoes radioactive decay.

The usefulness of an isotope depends on its specific properties. It would be incorrect to assume that all isotopes of uranium, cobalt or iodine can be substituted for one another in these applications.

Prelims focus

  • Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
  • Protium, deuterium and tritium contain 0, 1 and 2 neutrons respectively.
  • Carbon-12 is stable; carbon-14 and tritium are radioactive.
  • Argon-40 and calcium-40 are isobars.
  • Uranium-235 is associated with nuclear fission; cobalt-60 with radiotherapy; iodine-131 with thyroid treatment.
  • Trap: All isotopes of an element are not necessarily radioactive.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, printed pp. 52-54; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Nuclear Medicine, section on diagnostic and therapeutic radioisotopes, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Isotopes and Isobars: Same Element, Different Nuclear Composition

body:
What is radioactivity?

Some atomic nuclei are unstable. An unstable nucleus can change spontaneously into a more stable nuclear arrangement, releasing particles or electromagnetic energy. This process is called radioactive decay, and the property of undergoing such decay is called radioactivity.

The particles or energy emitted are forms of radiation. An atom that undergoes radioactive decay may change into an atom of a different element, depending on the type of decay.

Radioactivity is a property of certain unstable nuclei. Radiation is the energy or particles emitted or transmitted. Not every form of radiation comes from radioactive decay.

Ionising and non-ionising radiation

Ionising radiation carries sufficient energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules and create ions. Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and medical X-rays are important examples. Because ionisation can damage living cells and DNA, exposure must be controlled.

Visible light and ordinary radio waves are examples of non-ionising electromagnetic radiation. They do not normally have enough energy per photon to ionise atoms. Thus, the word radiation does not always mean radioactivity or a nuclear hazard.

The 3 main forms of radioactive emission

TypeNature and chargeTypical penetration and shielding
AlphaHelium nucleus containing 2 protons and 2 neutrons; charge +2Low penetration; stopped by paper or the outer dead layer of skin
BetaFast electron in beta-minus decay; charge -1Greater penetration than alpha; thin aluminium or suitable plastic can stop it
GammaHigh-energy electromagnetic radiation; no electric charge or rest massHighly penetrating; thick lead or concrete reduces its intensity

Alpha radiation is strongly ionising over a short distance. An external alpha source generally cannot penetrate intact skin deeply, but an alpha-emitting substance can be dangerous if inhaled or swallowed. Beta radiation can penetrate further and may damage skin. Gamma radiation can penetrate deeply, so external exposure can be significant.

The order of typical penetrating ability is alpha < beta < gamma. However, the biological danger cannot be ranked solely by penetration. The dose received and whether radioactive material enters the body are also important.

How radioactive decay changes a nucleus

In alpha decay, the nucleus emits 2 protons and 2 neutrons together. Its atomic number decreases by 2 and its mass number decreases by 4.

In beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton while an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted. The atomic number increases by 1, but the mass number remains unchanged. Beta radiation can also occur in other forms; the description here refers specifically to beta-minus decay.

In gamma emission, the nucleus releases excess energy as electromagnetic radiation. Its proton and neutron numbers remain unchanged, so gamma emission alone does not change the element or its mass number.

Half-life measures the rate of radioactive decay

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time required for half the radioactive nuclei in a sufficiently large sample to decay. Equivalently, the sample's activity falls to half its original value.

Suppose a large sample initially contains 80 units of radioactive material. After 1 half-life, approximately 40 units remain undecayed. After 2 half-lives, approximately 20 remain. After 3 half-lives, approximately 10 remain.

This is a statistical pattern. It does not mean that every individual nucleus has a fixed lifetime. It also does not mean that the material disappears completely after 1 or 2 half-lives. Each successive half-life removes half of what remains.

Different isotopes have different half-lives. Some decay quickly; others remain radioactive for very long periods. The choice of a medical radioisotope depends partly on how long it remains active and what radiation it emits.

Prelims focus

  • Alpha radiation consists of helium nuclei with 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
  • Beta-minus radiation consists of high-speed electrons emitted during nuclear decay.
  • Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, not charged particles.
  • Typical penetration increases from alpha to beta to gamma.
  • Half-life is the time for the undecayed radioactive nuclei, or activity, to decrease by half.
  • Trap: High penetration does not automatically mean the greatest hazard in every exposure situation.

[UK Government, Basic Concepts of Radiation, sections on alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and half-life, consulted 3 November 2026; UK Nuclear Decommissioning Authority, What Is Radiation?, sections on radioactive decay and shielding, consulted 3 November 2026.]
